name: Attention Residue
summary: The part of your attention that stays stuck on the previous task after you switch, and gets in the way of your focus on the new one.
explanation:
Attention residue is the part of your attention that stays on the previous task after you switch to a new one. Sophie Leroy coined the term in 2009. Her question was simple: why is it so hard to focus on the work in front of us when we keep moving between tasks?

In her experiments, people who switched away from a task they had not finished kept thinking about it, and they performed worse on the next task. Time pressure helped, which you might not expect. People who finished the first task under time pressure showed less residue, and they did better on the next task than both those who left it unfinished and those who finished it without time pressure. The likely reason is that a deadline pushes us to close the task in our heads, not just on paper. In a 2018 follow-up with Theresa Glomb, Leroy found two more things. Expecting time pressure when you return to an interrupted task increases residue. And writing a one-minute ready-to-resume plan before you switch reduces it.

The mechanism fits older findings. Unfinished tasks stay active in memory, which is the Zeigarnik effect. Task-set inertia describes how the previous task set keeps interfering with the next one. And the plan-making effect shows that a concrete plan for an unfinished goal quiets it.

Why does it matter? Because context switching costs more than the switch itself. Every half-finished task, message you glanced at, or project you "keep an eye on" leaves residue, and that residue follows you into the next block of work. At the end of the day, it also blocks psychological detachment. So finish a task or explicitly park it before you switch (i.e., write down where you are and what comes next). Batch shallow work and cut down on self-interruptions. Keep few projects active at the same time, and close the workday with a shutdown ritual.

One caveat: the core studies were lab experiments with about 80 undergraduates each. The idea is well grounded, but the exact size of the effect in real work is uncertain.

articles.title: Why Is It So Hard to Do My Work? The Challenge of Attention Residue When Switching Between Work Tasks
